title: An approach for monitoring temperature on fruit surface by means of thermal point cloud
author: Tsoulias, Jörissen, et al.
materials: After calibration, the phenotype sensing system was mounted on a circular conveyor platform, established in the experimental apple orchard (TechGarden), employing an electrical engine working with 50 Hz (DRN71, SEW Eurodrive, Germany) and stainless-steel chain with mechanical suspensions for varying plant sensors (Fig 1c). A real time kinematic global navigation satellite system (AgGPS 542, Trimble, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) is used to geo-reference the data and an inertial measurement unit (MTi-G-710, XSENS, Enschede, Netherlands) to acquire orientation information are arranged on the sensor frame. The root mean square error (RMSE) of orientation noted at 0.25° for roll (φ), pitch (θ) and yaw (ψ). Furthermore, an RTK-GNSS (AgGPS 542, Trimble, Sunnyvale, CA, USA) used for georeferencing each individual scanning profile of the 3D point cloud. The horizontal and vertical accuracy of the RTK-GNSS is ± 25 mm + 2 ppm and ± 37 mm + 2 ppm, respectively. The IMU is placed 0.3 m aside from the LiDAR sensor, while the receiver antenna of RTK-GNSS is mounted 0.6 m abive the laser scanner (Fig. 1). This phenotyping platform was established in a single row of the experimental apple orchard in 2020. The platform enables the automated monitoring of 109 trees in one row of 84 m length.

After mean centering, each Pi with P˜ value per nearest neighbor's set and decomposition of covariance matrix. The latter was decomposed based on the singular value decomposition, producing the eigenvalues (λ1, λ2, λ3), which were classified according to decreasing percentage of explained variance in the data. The eigenvalues were scaled between 0 and 100, allowing the comparison of different clusters. More specifically, the values closer to 100, the higher the likelihood for shape of points to be curved. The probability density function was performed to define the thresholds of curvature (Cth) and LiDAR's backscattered reflectance (Rth) defining the range of apple points in terms of C and backscattered reflectance (CA and RA). The points that fulfilled the criteria of Cth ≤ CA, and Rth ≤ RA were segmented and categorised as apples. This allowed to define the temperature values on the surface of apples by means of LiDAR (FSTLiDAR). The temperature on fruit surface was manually measured (FSTManual) (n = 285) with an infrared thermometer (Microscanner D501, Exergen, Watertown, USA) and compared with the correspondent averaged FSTLiDAR. The detected apples were categorised, in west and east, based on their position on the tree side.

A metal tree frame with dimensions 2 m × 0.30 m × 0.05 m was constructed to assess the measuring uncertainty of the phenotypic system in terms of temperature (Fig. 8). Five bars with 0.30 m distance from each other were placed horizontally on each side of a metal trunk. Sphere targets of 60 mm (n = 3) and 80 mm (n = 12) size were applied to assess the temperature derived by the phenotypic platform. The spheres were coated with white barium sulphate (BaSO4, CAS Number: 7727-43-7, Merck, Germany) and blackened urethane (S black, Avian Technologies, New London, NH, USA) for acquiring the minimum (SW) and maximum (SB) TLiDAR on the sphere surface. The phenotypic system was utilised to scan the metal frame indoors and outdoors in the orchard, and an infrared thermometer to manually acquire the temperature on the sphere surface (TManual).Fig. 8Representation of the metal tree frame of known distances with sphere targets.Fig 8

steps.title: Record orchard site and tree layout
steps.instruction: Note the experimental station location (52.466274° N, 12.57291° E), orchard slope (8 % southeast), tree cultivars (‘Gala’, ‘JonaPrince’, pollinator ‘Red Idared’), rootstock (M9), tree spacing (0.95 m), average height (2.5 m), and wire support configuration.

steps.title: Assemble sensor frame on linear conveyor
steps.instruction: Mount the rigid aluminium frame carrying the LiDAR and thermal camera on a 0.8 m linear tooth‑belt conveyor (Module 115/42, IEF Werner, Germany) equipped with a servo positioning controller (LV‑servoTEC S2).

substeps.instruction: Set conveyor forward speed to 20 mm s⁻¹ (± 0.05 mm accuracy).
Mount the 2D LiDAR (LMS‑511, Sick AG) vertically 0.7 m above ground; configure angular resolution 0.1667°, scanning frequency 25 Hz, scanning angle 180°, wavelength 905 nm.

Mount the thermal camera (A655sc, FLIR Systems) 0.2 m above the LiDAR; set resolution 640 × 480 px at 50 Hz, spectral range 7.5–14 µm, operational temperature –40 °C to 150 °C, thermal resolution < 0.05 °C, and attach lens T198065 (focal length 6.5 mm, diagonal 80°).
Connect LiDAR and camera via Ethernet to a laptop running LabVIEW NXG 5.1; connect the conveyor controller via RS‑232 using S2 Commander 4.1.4201.1.1.

steps.title: Perform intrinsic calibration of thermal camera
steps.instruction: Determine camera matrix and distortion parameters using an active light‑bulb calibration pattern.

substeps.instruction: Construct pattern: wooden board 500 mm × 600 mm with 30 × 12 V lightbulbs (4 mm diameter) arranged 5 × 6 grid, 100 mm spacing.
Place pattern in a window‑less, ventilated room at 15 °C.
Capture n images (dataset of 140 images; discard 10 with missing blobs).
Convert each raw thermal image to 8‑bit using a temperature range T (e.g., [20 °C, 60 °C]) and scale to full 8‑bit range.
Configure OpenCV SimpleBlobDetector with three sensitivity settings (s = 1, 2, 3) and the following thresholds (Table 1):
• Sensitivity 1: minThreshold 120, maxThreshold 220, thresholdStep 15, minArea 160, maxArea 230.
• Sensitivity 2: minThreshold 220, maxThreshold 150, thresholdStep 38, minArea 0, maxArea 350.
• Sensitivity 3: minThreshold 220, maxThreshold 200, thresholdStep 51, minArea 0, maxArea 220.
• Sensitivity 4: minThreshold 200, maxThreshold 510, thresholdStep 100, minArea 0, maxArea 100.

Run blob detection; if the required 30 blobs are not found, repeat with the next sensitivity; after three sensitivities fail, rescale image temperature range down by 5 °C and retry; after four temperature ranges and all sensitivities fail, mark image as failed.

Compute blob centers and radii; use detected 2D points together with known 3D positions of lightbulbs to solve for focal lengths (fx, fy), principal point (cx, cy), and distortion coefficients (k1‑k3, p1‑p2) via OpenCV calibration routine.
Resulting intrinsic RMSE = 0.33 px.

steps.title: Perform extrinsic calibration between camera and LiDAR
steps.instruction: Determine rotation R and translation t linking LiDAR coordinates to camera image plane.

substeps.instruction: Record 21 scans of the calibration pattern at different positions on the linear conveyor; note that 6 scans are unusable due to pattern cut‑off.
For each valid scan:
a. Crop point cloud with an axis‑aligned bounding box to remove ceiling, floor, and walls.
b. Apply Open3D RANSAC plane detection to isolate the dominant plane (the pattern).
c. Verify plane dimensions match the 500 mm × 600 mm board; discard mismatches.
d. Downsample the plane points (voxel grid), then perform PCA to obtain initial orientation T_initial and centroid.
e. Generate a synthetic perfect model of the pattern, roughly align using T_initial, and refine alignment with ICP to obtain correction T_corr.
f. Compute final transformation T_final = T_initial × T_corr, yielding rotation R and translation t.
g. Extract 3D coordinates L of each lightbulb from the transformed point cloud.
h. Minimise reprojection error Σ‖o_i – ô(A,D,R,t,L_i)‖² to refine R and t.
Compute RMSE for each scan; average RMSE across all scans = 1.82 px; select scan 6 with lowest RMSE = 1.25 px for subsequent use.

steps.title: Fuse temperature data with 3D point cloud
steps.instruction: Assign a temperature value to each LiDAR point using the calibrated intrinsic and extrinsic parameters.

substeps.instruction: Project every LiDAR point into the thermal image using the camera matrix A and extrinsic (R,t).
If the projected pixel lies inside the image, assign the pixel’s temperature value to the point.
If the projected pixel lies outside, assign a placeholder temperature of –10 °C.

steps.title: Mount phenotyping platform on circular conveyor in orchard
steps.instruction: Transfer the calibrated sensor frame to the field‑ready circular conveyor system.

substeps.instruction: Install the frame on the circular conveyor (TechGarden) driven by a 50 Hz electric engine (DRN71, SEW Eurodrive) with stainless‑steel chain suspension.
Attach RTK‑GNSS (AgGPS 542, Trimble) and IMU (MTi‑G‑710, XSENS) to the frame; place IMU 0.3 m beside LiDAR and GNSS antenna 0.6 m above LiDAR.
Verify orientation RMSE = 0.25° for roll, pitch, yaw; GNSS horizontal accuracy ±25 mm + 2 ppm, vertical ±37 mm + 2 ppm.
Position the platform in a single orchard row (84 m length, 109 trees).

steps.title: Acquire orchard scans and thermal images
steps.instruction: Collect synchronized LiDAR point clouds and thermal frames while the conveyor moves around the trees.

steps.title: Segment apples from 3D point cloud
steps.instruction: Identify individual fruit points and extract their surface temperatures.

substeps.instruction: Apply rigid translation and rotation to align opposite tree sides; refine alignment with ICP.
Estimate stem positions for each of n = 20 trees using a bivariate point‑density histogram; generate a cylindrical region around each stem to isolate a tree.
For each tree point cloud, compute curvature C for every point using k‑nearest‑neighbors (k unspecified).
Calculate mean point P̃ = (1/N) Σ_i P_i, where N is the number of points in the tree.
Perform singular value decomposition on the covariance matrix of the local neighbourhood to obtain eigenvalues λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ λ₃; scale eigenvalues to 0‑100.
Define curvature threshold C_th and reflectance threshold R_th from probability density functions; classify a point as apple if C_th ≤ C_A and R_th ≤ R_A.
Label detected apples as belonging to the west or east side based on their position.

steps.title: Validate temperature measurements with metal frame
steps.instruction: Assess measurement uncertainty using a calibrated metal tree frame and sphere targets.

substeps.instruction: Build metal frame (2 m × 0.30 m × 0.05 m) with five horizontal bars spaced 0.30 m apart on each side of a metal trunk.
Place sphere targets: three 60 mm spheres (white barium sulfate coating, BaSO₄, CAS 7727‑43‑7, Merck) and twelve 80 mm spheres (black urethane coating, S‑black, Avian Technologies).
Scan the frame indoors and outdoors; record manual sphere temperatures with an infrared thermometer (Microscanner D501, Exergen).
Compute descriptive statistics (min, max, mean, SD) for LiDAR‑derived temperatures (T_LiDAR) on white (SW) and black (SB) spheres.

Indoor results: SB max 19.84 °C, min 19.72 °C, mean 19.69 °C, SD 0.08 °C, MBE 0.02 °C, RMSE 0.02 °C, R²_adj 0.95; SW max 19.82 °C, min 19.54 °C, mean 19.84 °C, SD 0.07 °C, MBE 0.01 °C, RMSE 0.01 °C, R²_adj 0.94.

Outdoor results: SB max 22.31 °C, min 20.81 °C, mean 22.20 °C, SD 0.67 °C, MBE ‑0.03 °C, RMSE 0.11 °C, R²_adj 0.97; SW max 19.63 °C, min 19.18 °C, mean 19.39 °C, SD 0.18 °C, MBE 0.01 °C, RMSE 0.04 °C, R²_adj 0.95.

steps.title: Analyze fruit temperature results
steps.instruction: Compare LiDAR‑derived fruit surface temperature (FST_LiDAR) with manual infrared measurements (FST_Manual).

substeps.instruction: Collect data from 285 apples 130 days after full bloom; note that tree organs above 2 m have T_LiDAR ≤ 18.2 °C; stem points mean 20.6 °C ± 0.65 °C.
Detect apples (272) with 89.7 % F1 score.
FST_LiDAR range 16 – 22 °C; manual vs LiDAR regression: west side R²_adj 0.91, RMSE 0.25 °C; east side R²_adj 0.99, RMSE 0.01 °C.
Mean east‑side FST_LiDAR 18.8 ± 0.75 °C; west‑side 18.3 ± 0.61 °C.
Perform descriptive statistics and regression analysis in MATLAB R2018b.
